pages.title: Bandung principles, NAM origins and agenda phases
pages.summary: India hosted the Asian Relations Conference in 1946, and the 1955 Bandung conference produced 10 principles that became NAM's fundamentals, with 25 countries at the first NAM conference in Belgrade in 1961. NAM's agenda moved from anti-imperialism (the 1960s, its most successful phase) to the NIEO at Algiers 1973 and nuclear disarmament in the 1980s, both without success, then a question mark over its purpose after the Cold War.

pages.title: NAM in the 1990s: re-invention and criticism
pages.summary: After the Cold War NAM appeared anachronistic, and although some members such as Egypt suggested ending it, the Jakarta summit decided to re-invent it. Criticisms are rhetorical declarations, an unwieldy size, no role in the Iraq-Kuwait crisis or India-Pakistan disputes, and division into pro-Soviet and pro-US members, leading to the label Team B of USSR.

pages.title: NAM's identity crisis and arguments for relevance
pages.summary: NAM was called a club of dictators, lacks an organisational structure beyond a New York secretariat, and took no concrete initiative on Libya and Syria. Rashid ud din Khan calls it a timeless platform of developing countries, citing the 2006 Havana declaration against unilateralism, while C. Raja Mohan says it is in a coma and should have declared Mission accomplished.

pages.title: India's stance on NAM and its relevance
pages.summary: Raja Mohan thought dissolving NAM after the Cold War would have been a graceful exit. The present Indian government has fewer illusions about NAM, as the PM skipped the 2016 Venezuela summit, yet NAM stays relevant to India as a platform of natural leadership, common interests with developing countries and support for UNSC membership.

pages.title: NAM needs leadership; origins of IBSA
pages.summary: NAM needs vision, an agenda and re-invention, and only India can lead it as its brain child and as a bridge between North and South and South and South. Introduces IBSA (India, Brazil, South Africa), conceived by Yashwant Sinha out of dissatisfaction with developed countries' attitude and WTO policies.

pages.title: IBSA's three pillars and the IBSA Fund
pages.summary: Developing countries pushed for the Doha Development Agenda without result, so IBSA was created by the Brasilia Declaration in 2003, with summits since 2005. Its pillars are geo-political reform of global governance, the IBSA Fund ($1 mn per country, demand-driven, no conditionalities, MDG award 2010) and civil society involvement.

pages.title: Why IBSA suits India; China's response
pages.summary: IBSA helps India regain ground among developing countries and build soft power, and the West has no negative attitude to it as it does to NAM, although the summit due in 2012 was postponed. India kept China out of IBSA as a platform of democracy, while China inducted South Africa into BRICS in 2010.

pages.title: IBSA versus NAM; BRICS origins and importance
pages.summary: IBSA and NAM are both important and complement each other. BRICS, an acronym coined by Jim O'Neil, evolved into a geopolitical platform from its first summit in Yekaterinburg in 2009, and matters for its huge market, resources, manpower and the UNSC and military weight of its members.

pages.title: BRICS achievements and dim prospects
pages.summary: BRICS has produced the New Development Bank and the Contingency Reserve Arrangement, but its prospects are now dim. China is slowing, Russia and Brazil are in recession, intra-BRICS trade is low, and members have conflicting concerns, as at Goa 2016 where neither China nor Russia backed India on Pakistan-sponsored terrorism.

pages.title: BRICS or IBSA priority; India-Africa kinship
pages.summary: India's priority should be IBSA because BRICS is dominated by China, though a divorce is too early to predict. Opens India and Africa as linked by history, geography, shared challenges and demographic dividend, with Africa now a continent of hope and renaissance.

flashcards.front: What is the link between the 1955 Bandung conference and NAM, and where was NAM's first conference held?
flashcards.back: Bandung (Indonesia, 1955) was the first Afro-Asian conference and produced the 10 Bandung principles, which became NAM's fundamental principles. The first NAM conference was held in Belgrade, Yugoslavia, in 1961 with 25 countries.

flashcards.front: How did NAM's agenda evolve from the 1960s to the 1980s, and how successful was each phase?
flashcards.back: 1960s: anti-imperialism and anti-racialism, its most successful phase. 1970s: the New International Economic Order resolution at Algiers 1973 against neo-colonialism, no success. 1980s: nuclear disarmament, no success.

flashcards.front: How did NAM respond to the post-Cold War question about its relevance?
flashcards.back: NAM appeared an anachronistic relic and some members such as Egypt wanted it ended, but the Jakarta summit chose to re-invent it as a movement for developing-world concerns. It argued that having one superpower does not mean aligning with it.

flashcards.front: What are the main criticisms of NAM made in the notes?
flashcards.back: Its declarations stayed rhetoric, it grew too big and disparate, and it had no role in Iraq's invasion of Kuwait or India-Pakistan conflicts. It was divided, called Team B of USSR and a club of dictators, and has only a secretariat in New York.

flashcards.front: Why does NAM remain relevant for India according to the notes?
flashcards.back: It is a platform where India has natural leadership, India shares common interests with developing nations from Doha to Paris as home to the largest number of poor, and NAM support matters for India's bid for UNSC membership.

flashcards.front: What is IBSA, when was it formed and what are its three pillars?
flashcards.back: IBSA (India, Brazil, South Africa) was formed by the Brasilia Declaration in 2003, with summits since 2005. Its pillars are geo-political reform of global governance, the IBSA Fund ($1 mn from each country, demand-driven, no conditionalities) and civil society involvement.

flashcards.front: Why are BRICS prospects considered dim despite the New Development Bank?
flashcards.back: Beyond the New Development Bank and Contingency Reserve Arrangement, China is slowing, Russia and Brazil are in recession and intra-BRICS trade is low. Members have conflicting concerns and lack mortar, as at Goa 2016 when neither China nor Russia backed India on terrorism.

answers.question: Critically evaluate the achievements and failures of NAM and discuss its relevance for India.
answers.intro: Born in the Cold War from leaders like Nehru, Sukarno, Tito and Nasser, NAM is the largest developing-country platform outside the UNGA. After 1991 it faced questions about its raison d'etre, and its record is judged mixed.
body: Achievements: from the 1955 Bandung principles to the 1961 Belgrade conference, NAM's anti-imperialist and anti-racialist 1960s were its most successful phase, when newly independent states stayed outside military blocs.

Failures: the NIEO resolution at Algiers 1973 and 1980s nuclear disarmament brought no success; NAM had no role in Iraq's invasion of Kuwait or India-Pakistan disputes, stayed rhetorical and divided into pro-Soviet and pro-US members, and was labelled Team B of the USSR.

Structural weakness: it grew too big and diffuse, was called a club of dictators demanding democracy internationally, has only a secretariat in New York, and took no concrete initiative on Libya and Syria; C. Raja Mohan says it is in a coma.

Relevance for India: the Jakarta summit re-invented NAM and the 2006 Havana declaration opposed unilateralism; for India it offers natural leadership, common cause with developing countries and support for UNSC membership, though the present government treats it mainly as a legacy.
answers.conclusion: NAM's record is strong on decolonisation but weak on delivery. It remains relevant as an existing platform of the South, yet only fresh leadership, a concrete agenda and complementary groupings such as IBSA can prevent it fading into rhetoric.

answers.question: Compare IBSA, BRICS and NAM as platforms for India's South-South cooperation. Which should India prioritise?
answers.intro: NAM, IBSA and BRICS are three platforms for India's engagement with the Global South. The notes treat IBSA as smart and democratic, NAM as large but diffused, and BRICS as China-dominated with uncertain cohesion.
body: IBSA: formed by the 2003 Brasilia Declaration, an idea of Yashwant Sinha born of dissatisfaction with developed countries' stance on developmental needs and the Doha agenda. Its pillars are geo-political reform of global governance, the IBSA Fund and civil society.

IBSA Fund: $1 mn from each member, demand-driven with no conditionalities, unlike the World Bank, funding waste management, sports, irrigation and health projects in Burundi, Vietnam, Cape Verde and Palestine, and winning the 2010 MDG award.

Why IBSA suits India: it regains lost ground among developing countries, draws no western hostility as NAM does, builds soft power, and is a democratic platform that India kept free of China, though its summit due in 2012 has been postponed.

BRICS: a Jim O'Neil acronym that evolved into a geopolitical platform, first meeting at Yekaterinburg in 2009, with the New Development Bank and Contingency Reserve Arrangement, but low intra-BRICS trade, a slowing China, India-China tension and no shared mortar make prospects dim.
answers.conclusion: The notes hold that IBSA and NAM complement rather than supplement each other, while BRICS is China-dominated, so India's priority should lean towards IBSA. Reviving the stalled IBSA summits would test India's commitment to South-South leadership.
